perblock.scientificAssessment: Both texts identify field source and induced-output winding, distinguish emf from flux magnitude, and explicitly require series/in-phase turns and fixed rotation rate/flux waveform for the stated amplitude comparisons. Turn-number proportionality is read for the same per-turn flux in the described winding. Phi_m=BS is confined to the earlier uniform-field rotating-loop model, not arbitrary magnetic circuits. B in tesla times S in square metres gives flux in webers; flux-change rate gives volts.
perblock.bilingualAssessment: Field source, rotating-loop model, series addition, in-phase condition, fixed-rate/waveform qualifiers, per-turn flux amplitude and Section 21 reference agree. The exact source formula and its maximum-flux meaning are retained in both languages.

perblock.scientificAssessment: Rotor means rotating part and stator stationary part. The inner/outer core, slots and horizontal/vertical axis describe the source design, not all generators. An air gap can belong to a closed magnetic circuit without continuous steel. Smaller clearance lowers magnetic reluctance and favors flux at the same excitation while preserving mechanical noncontact; no unconditional maximum-flux guarantee is carried forward.
perblock.bilingualAssessment: The two functional cores/windings, usual inner rotating core, stationary outer part, axis alternatives, noncontact air gap and fixed-excitation limitation agree. Both narrow the source's broad construction claim to the described iron-core design.

perblock.scientificAssessment: Conducting cores exposed to changing linked flux support eddy currents and dissipative heating. Insulated thin laminations restrict current loops and reduce the associated loss; neither text says every rotor experiences the same time-varying flux, that all cores must be laminated, or that all generator losses disappear.
perblock.bilingualAssessment: Conductivity, changing-flux condition, heating/efficiency consequence, mutually insulated thin steel sheets and reduction rather than elimination of loss agree. The conditional construction scope is matched.

perblock.scientificAssessment: The source's earlier coreless rotating loop and stationary permanent magnet are preserved as a text description. Reversing which part rotates can induce emf in a stationary loop provided its linked flux changes. Mere rotation of an arbitrary magnet is not asserted sufficient; the explicit changing-flux condition supplies the needed assumption.
perblock.bilingualAssessment: Earlier Figure 26 reference, coreless rotor, stationary permanent field source, rotating-magnet alternative and time-varying-flux condition agree.
perblock.approvalLimit: Text-only PASS against raw p0091#3; no inspection or approval of historical fig-26 or its visual correspondence.

perblock.scientificAssessment: Both versions correctly distinguish the rotating DC-excited field winding from the stationary stator output winding. Excitation brushes are not main-output brushes. Slip rings maintain field-winding connections, and the same-shaft auxiliary DC generator is correctly called an exciter. The source's confused exciter-stator wording is not propagated as a general fact. The smaller excitation current and brushed construction are explicitly source-arrangement claims, not universal generator requirements.
perblock.bilingualAssessment: Electrical roles, DC excitation, stationary brushes, relative excitation/load current, same-shaft exciter and design limitations agree. One neutral source quantity is missing from English: source and Chinese explicitly specify two contact rings, separately connected to the two field-winding ends; English only says plural slip rings connect to the ends.
perblock.approvalLimit: Scientific mechanism PASS covers prose only, not the rings/brushes depiction in unreviewed fig-57.

perblock.scientificAssessment: A rotating permanent magnet needs no excitation current; a stationary output winding needs no rotating output-current contact. Hence the specified design needs neither excitation nor output slip rings/brushes. This is confined to that topology, not all small generators or all other possible electrical contacts.
perblock.bilingualAssessment: Small-generator possibility, permanent-magnet excitation distinction, stationary load winding, no-ring/no-brush conclusion and exclusion of a universal small-generator claim agree.

perblock.scientificAssessment: For the described rotating-field generator, the stator-linked flux changes and a circulating electric field acts along the stationary winding. This correctly describes induction without wire motion. Constant linked flux alone cannot produce the stated transformer emf; neither version falsely requires stator motion or treats nonzero flux magnitude as sufficient.
perblock.bilingualAssessment: Rotating field, time-dependent linked flux, circulating electric field, stationary wire and rate-of-change rather than flux-magnitude distinction agree. Circulating electric field faithfully translates the source concept without introducing fluid motion.

perblock.scientificAssessment: Uniform-field rotating-loop period is correctly qualified by constant speed and changing field-normal angle. A two-pole rotating field gives one electrical cycle per revolution. Alternating 4/6/8 poles give 2/3/4 pole pairs, electrical periods of 1/2, 1/3, 1/4 of mechanical period and the same fractions of two-pole speed at fixed electrical frequency. The prose avoids the erroneous universal reading that each individually identified pole must pass the winding 50 times per second. The general relation is read in the described alternating-pole rotating-field generator context.
perblock.bilingualAssessment: All ten source math spans, 50 hertz, 50 revolutions/second, 3000 revolutions/minute, 1/50 second, pole/pair distinction, period/speed fractions, water-turbine motivation and rpm-to-rps conversion agree. Historical plant identity and source-era 62.5 rpm/48-pair attribution are preserved in both languages, with explicit exclusion of current-equipment and other-grid claims.
reviewerQuantityChecks: 50 revolutions/second multiplied by 60 seconds/minute gives 3000 revolutions/minute.
1/50 second is 0.02 second and corresponds to 50 full electrical cycles/second.
At 50 Hz, 4/6/8 poles require 1500/1000/750 rpm respectively in the described rotating-field relation.
62.5 revolutions/minute multiplied by 48 pole pairs and divided by 60 seconds/minute gives 50 Hz; 48 pole pairs means 96 poles, not 48 poles.
